title: Local Redundancy: An Information-Theoretic Measure of Plasticity from Synthetic Memorization
claim: A principled measure of capacity to adapt is bounded by a cheap gradient quantity and predicts downstream performance better than common heuristics.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: two circles, geometric blob with formula, bar chart
description: Three panels. (a) 'Plasticity as Information Radius' shows two circles: a large blue one labeled 'High Plasticity' with a long arrow for radius R_n** (large), and a small red one labeled 'Low Plasticity' with a short arrow (small). Scattered dots mark reachable distributions around a center P_θ0. (b) 'Memorization Gradient Lower Bound' shows a gray irregular blob around a center point P_θ0. A short black arrow points to P_{θ0+ε∇L} on the boundary, a dotted line continues to a 'Memorization dataset' point, and a dashed brown arrow marks the radius R_n**(θ0, ε). A yellow box below holds the inequality R ≥ ε·E[||∇L||²]. (c) 'Correlation with Future Task Performance' is a bar chart of correlation improvement (%) with error bars. The teal 'Local Redundancy (Ours)' bar is tallest at 8.9, followed by gray bars for Dist. from Init, Weight Norm, Dead Neurons and Train Grad Norm. The eye goes first to the circles, then to the highlighted bar.
caption: Local redundancy: a principled, computable measure of plasticity. (a) Redundancy measures the information radius of a model class: a plastic network can reach many distributions (large radius); a rigid network cannot (small radius). (b) The expected squared gradient norm on synthetic memorization data lower-bounds local redundancy (Theorem [ref]), requiring only a single backward pass to compute. (c) Local redundancy predicts downstream performance better than existing plasticity heuristics in continual learning; see Section [ref] for transfer learning.
abstract: Plasticity -- a neural network's ability to adapt to new tasks -- is critical for continual and transfer learning. Existing measures, such as effective rank, dead neuron fraction, and weight norm, lack theoretical grounding and correlate poorly with performance on new tasks. We introduce local redundancy, an information-theoretic measure derived from universal compression theory. We define local redundancy as the worst-case redundancy of a local model family -- parameters in an infinitesimal neighborhood along gradient directions -- and show this is a principled measure of plasticity. Although local redundancy is intractable to compute exactly, we prove that the expected squared gradient norm on a synthetic memorization task provides an efficiently computable lower bound. Experiments on continual image classification and time series transfer learning demonstrate that local redundancy predicts downstream performance better than existing measures and enables pretraining checkpoint selection where validation loss plateaus.
